viral_ticker_tweets.full_text_en:
We're sharing new data on how AI is changing research at OpenAI.

We find researchers' AI use continues to rise exponentially, and agents are completing longer tasks, but human involvement remains central in research. Researchers are also spending more time on safety and alignment, with human effort in these areas growing faster than in any other individual research area.

This report aims to increase transparency around research acceleration and inform the governance of increasingly capable AI. We believe that AI labs should be required to track and publicly report indicators of recursive self-improvement (RSI): the process by which AI accelerates the development of future AI systems. 

Our hope is that this expanded report will help sustain and advance shared measurement norms across the industry.

https://t.co/xyGPcCkPCK
viral_ticker_tweets.full_text_zh:
我们正在 OpenAI 上分享有关人工智能如何改变研究的新数据。

我们发现研究人员对人工智能的使用持续呈指数级增长，智能体正在完成更长的任务，但人类的参与仍然是研究的核心。研究人员也在安全和协调上花费了更多的时间，人类在这些领域的努力比任何其他单独的研究领域增长得更快。

本报告旨在提高研究加速的透明度，并为日益强大的人工智能的治理提供信息。我们认为，应该要求人工智能实验室跟踪并公开报告递归自我改进（RSI）指标：人工智能加速未来人工智能系统开发的过程。

我们希望这份扩展报告将有助于维持和推进整个行业的共享衡量规范。

viral_ticker_tweets.full_text_en:
Good morning CT🧡

What happens when one AI agent needs a service that another agent can provide?

@termix_ai is building a system that lets AI agents find jobs, work for each other and get paid through AACP.

For example, a trading agent might need market research, while a separate research agent can provide that service.

With AACP, the process can involve job discovery, bidding, escrow, task delivery, verification and payment settlement.

Both agents can have onchain identities and build reputations through completed work.

This goes beyond simply listing AI agents in a marketplace. 

It creates a structure for agents to find work, provide services and get paid.

That’s the kind of infrastructure the growing agent economy needs.

top_three.summary_en: ByteDance co-founder Zhang Yiming has become the richest person in Asia with a net worth exceeding $105 billion, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index. His wealth surged following valuation markups by institutional investors like BlackRock and Fidelity, coupled with ByteDance's aggressive pivot toward AI development, including Doubao, Seedance, and a massive 10-trillion-parameter model.
paragraphs: ByteDance co-founder Zhang Yiming, in a portrait released by the company in 2021.

ByteDance co-founder Zhang Yiming is now Asia’s richest person, with an estimated fortune of more than $105bn, putting him ahead of Indian industrialist Gautam Adani, according to Bloomberg. The ranking comes from the Bloomberg Billionaires Index, and Zhang, 43, has never held the top spot before.

The figure is an estimate, and other trackers disagree. Forbes’ real-time list put Zhang’s net worth at $84bn on Wednesday. The gap comes largely from how each list values ByteDance, a private company whose shares do not trade publicly. Bloomberg applies a 10% risk discount to its valuation.

Investor valuations drove the latest jump. Zhang’s wealth rose by more than $12bn this month after Bloomberg analyzed the latest marks that BlackRock, Fidelity Investments, and T. Rowe Price put on their ByteDance holdings. In June, the index had already lifted him past Mukesh Ambani into second place, after Bloomberg cut its ByteDance discount from 25% once the company’s US restructuring was settled.

That restructuring nearly went the other way. ByteDance spent much of last year facing a possible US shutdown of TikTok, before handing control of the app’s American business to a venture led by Oracle and Silver Lake in January. Since then, the company has leaned harder into AI, with the Doubao chatbot and the Seedance video generator, alongside a 10-trillion-parameter model now in training.
“He plays his cards right,” Lian Jye Su, chief analyst at research firm Omdia, told Bloomberg.“He stayed on course and then continued to double down on AI investment.”

Su said Zhang kept backing AI development even as US lawmakers questioned TikTok chief executive Shou Chew in 2023, and that ByteDance’s store of social media data could in theory help it train models.
He called AI ByteDance’s biggest opportunity since its video platform, and fierce competition in China its biggest risk.

Adani’s slide explains the other half of the swap. His fortune peaked at about $120bn in June, Bloomberg reported, before an MSCI index rebalancing wiped about $15bn off his group’s market value at the end of August. A wider selloff, driven by rising oil prices and bond yields, pushed the shares lower still.

Zhang’s estimated wealth has grown about eightfold since March 2019, when Bloomberg first valued it at $13bn. He was already China’s richest person, and he now sits above Adani, Ambani, and Uniqlo founder Tadashi Yanai, fortunes built on ports, energy, and retail. The same boom has also made founders of Chinese chipmakers billionaires, even though those companies have yet to turn a profit, Bloomberg reported last week.

The ranking lands in a week when Beijing has been publicly defending its AI ambitions. China’s commerce ministry dismissed calls by US AI executives to slow frontier development as a bid for technological hegemony, and China’s richest person, whose fortune increasingly rests on AI, is now also Asia’s richest person.

top_three.summary_en: North American manufacturers are accelerating robot adoption to mitigate severe labor shortages, with Q3 2026 orders reaching 11,000 units, a 25% year-on-year increase. paragraphs: American companies are racing to install more industrial robots in factories and warehouses, as rising costs and worsening labour shortages threaten to choke off a nascent US manufacturing boom.

North American companies ordered almost 11,000 robots in the third quarter of 2026, up 25 per cent on the same period last year, according to the Association for Advancing Automation (A3). Orders of collaborative robots, or “cobots”, rose by 56 per cent.

Peggy Johnson, chief executive of Agility, a humanoid robotics company that listed on the Nasdaq this month, said that many manufacturing firms were facing “an existential problem with the labour that they can’t get”.

“There’s an older workforce doing manual, repetitive jobs that is retiring, we have a younger workforce that is not seeking those jobs, and then we have a government that is reshoring and that’s increasing the need for those jobs,” Johnson told the FT.

Successive US administrations have used a combination of generous tax credits and punitive tariffs to encourage companies to “reshore” manufacturing amid concerns over post-industrial decline in America’s heartlands and increasing competition from China.
Along with a post-Covid desire to reduce dependence on fragile global supply chains, the push has driven hundreds of billions of dollars of investment into US manufacturing over the past decade.

But rising inflation and President Donald Trump’s erratic application of tariffs have caused spending on manufacturing-related construction to fall since 2025, while employment in the sector has remained broadly flat.

Mike Conway, a partner at McKinsey who specialises in advising industrial companies, said that rather than building new factories, most US-based manufacturers were looking to unlock the “latent capacity” in existing facilities, including through automation.
“Given the need to scale, we’re seeing automation becoming the new normal,” he said.

Industrial robots range from humanoids to robot arms, cobots and so-called “gantry robots” that can ferry goods along perpendicular axes. Advocates argue they free human employees from “dull, dirty and dangerous” tasks such as routine inspections, lifting heavy items or handling hazardous materials.

Traditionally, only very large manufacturers such as carmakers have been able to deploy robots at a scale necessary to justify their cost. But technological advances, including the ability to train robots in virtual environments, have lowered barriers to entry for much smaller companies.
Sebastian Montalvo, chief executive of Texas-based aerospace and defence supplier M3 Aerospace, said that automation would allow his company, which employs 11 staff, to grow faster with fewer people.
“How we operate now is we have one operator, one machine, but I think with technology and robotics we may have one operator, five machines,” he said.

Alex Shikany, executive vice-president of A3, noted that whereas automotive companies had historically placed the bulk of North American robot orders, non-auto sectors including logistics, agriculture, life sciences and electronics together now account for more than half the sector.
“It bodes well for the robotics industry as we move forward because it’s less reliant on just one type of customer,” he said.
However, some experts argue that the speed of automation in the US is still not fast enough to make the country internationally competitive.

Robert Atkinson, founder and senior fellow at the Information Technology and Innovation Foundation think-tank, said that with US labour costs so much higher than in China, American companies should be automating even more aggressively.

“We need to double, triple the amount of robotic automation within five to eight years, or I believe we will lose a significant share of what remains of our manufacturing to China,” he said. “But we’re nowhere near.”

Analysts note that most of the robots being installed in the US come from abroad, feeding a tension in the Trump administration’s policies between its stated desire to revive US manufacturing, and its unhappiness about a surge in robots being brought into the country.The White House said last month that the Department of Commerce had found that “robotics, industrial machinery and their components” are being imported into the US “in such quantities . . . as to threaten to impair the national security of the United States”.But it added that it was holding off on applying extra tariffs on national security grounds because the US “still produces less robotics and industrial equipment than it consumes” and “lacks the capacity to satisfy the need for robotics and industrial machinery with domestic sources”.

Experts note an irony whereby the same shortage of skills that is driving companies to automate is likely to undermine US automation efforts. According to a recent labour shortage index compiled by the Alliance For America’s Skilled Trades, technicians needed to install and maintain automated systems are in shorter supply than almost any other category of skilled worker.
Agility’s Johnson believes that demand from companies for robots that can operate at facilities designed for human workers will continue to grow.
But the ITIF’s Atkinson warns that investing in robots to eke out incremental productivity gains at old facilities will not revive American manufacturing.
“When you build new things from scratch, you put in global state of the art equipment and technology — that’s what we see the Chinese doing,” he said.
“But we’re sort of retrofitting existing plants and it’s just harder to do. Maybe in 25 or 30 years we’ll have built everything we need, but we can’t wait that long.”

topic_focus.summary_zh: Meta旗下AI代理Muse在运行过程中，被证实存在跨账户信息混淆及非法提取加密隐私数据的严重漏洞。该事件揭露了Meta在将AI代理深度嵌入业务生态时，对其底层权限隔离和隐私安全架构的把控严重不足，引发行业对于“黑盒”模型合规性的强烈质疑。
topic_focus.summary_en: Meta’s Muse agent has been confirmed to exhibit cross-account data leaking and unauthorized extraction of encrypted information. The incident exposes critical failures in Meta’s privilege isolation and privacy architecture during deep deployment, sparking industry-wide skepticism regarding the compliance of 'black-box' agent models.

perspective_con.point_en: Cross-account leakage isn't just a bug; it represents a fundamental architecture flaw in agent permission design. Mass-deploying without rigorous security audits is utterly irresponsible.

linked_tweets.author: Aaron Levie
linked_tweets.content_zh:
不管它叫什么，我们的工作显然正在进入人工智能代理的另一个时代。

我们很快就从为您提供快速答案的代理跃升至今天您在一组任务中编排的代理。但是，由于智能体既可以扇出并并行工作，可以处理更大的环境，能够进行长时间运行的工作，并且具有更高水平的功能，我们正在进入人工智能为我们做的事情的另一个层面。

我们很快就能够为代理提供一组目标，他们可以出去设计实现该目标的最佳解决方案，同时还可以根据其所构建的内容的持续执行不断改进它。显然，这将从工程开始，因为我们看到几乎每个新代理时代都首先出现最佳实践。

但对其他知识工作的影响可能相当巨大。您将告诉代理改进您的客户入职工作流程以实现特定的目标；或者让代理人去降低您的业务风险；或持续改善您的安全状况。

这些自主系统将能够实现一系列目标、设计最佳结果、测试和迭代、部署，然后优化其持续构建的任何内容。重要的是，这会带来人类以前根本无法实现的结果。这将导致人工智能的生产力达到新的水平。
linked_tweets.content_en:
Regardless of what it’s called, we’re clearly moving to yet another era of AI agents in our work. 

We’ve quickly jumped from agents that spit out a quick answer for you, to today agents that you orchestrate inside of a set of tasks. But as agents can both fan out and work in parallel, handle much larger context, be able to do long running work, and have far greater levels of capabilities, we’re entering yet another level of what we can have AI do for us.

We’ll soon be able to give agents a set of goals, and they can go out and design the best solution for that goal, while also continuously improving it based on the ongoing execution of whatever it built. This will obviously start with engineering because that’s where we’re seeing the best practices emerge first in almost every new era of agents. 

But the impact can be quite massive across the rest of knowledge work. You’ll tell an agent to improve your client onboarding workflow to achieve a certain targeted goal; or have agents go reduce risk in your business; or improve your security posture on an ongoing basis.

These autonomous systems will be able to take on a set of goals, design the best outcome, test and iterate, deploy, and then optimize whatever it built on an ongoing basis. Importantly, this leads to outcomes and results that humans literally couldn’t have accomplished before. This will lead to fairly new levels of productivity with AI.

Ted Sarandos’ handpicked consigliere is tasked with reinventing the streamer — while his boss promises Wall Street that nothing is changing.

Reed Hastings found about Netflix’s big shake-up the same time everyone else did. The Netflix founder (he officially exited the board over the summer) told a rapt audience at the Masters of Scale Summit in San Francisco in late October that the mass layoffs, the exit of content chief Bela Bajaria and the surprise announcement of Peter Rice as its new head
news.summary_en: Netflix co-CEO Ted Sarandos has appointed former Disney Entertainment Chairman and Fox executive Peter Rice as the new Chief Content Officer, succeeding Bela Bajaria to overhaul the streamer's content strategy. With his proven track record in scaling FX and Hulu, Rice is tasked with shifting Netflix’s output from quantity-driven models toward a mix of commercial viability and high-end prestige productions.

news.author: Dana Goldstein
news.content_snippet:

news.summary_en: University students and faculty globally are protesting the integration of generative AI through petitions, religious exemption filings, and manifestos. The movement seeks to curtail institutional partnerships with AI vendors like OpenAI and Google, citing concerns over the erosion of critical thinking and the intrinsic value of human-centric education.
paragraphs: Last March, a handful of students at Transylvania University created a petition, attempting to slow the advance of artificial intelligence on their campus. It asked the administration to cancel chatbot licenses with A.I. giants and instead invest the money in “human-centered education.”
About a third of the college’s students signed on.

Transylvania, in Lexington, Ky., is tiny, with under 1,000 students. But across the country and the globe, there has been a swell of campus resistance to A.I., including a growing group of conscientious objectors who refuse to use A.I. at all.
Polls show the vast majority of American students use chatbots for school work. College leaders have generally embraced A.I., saying it is key to preparing students for the work force.
But as A.I. use grows, more students and faculty are sounding alarms and trying to slow it down.

Much of the opposition comes from the political left, and focuses on how A.I. could harm the environment, diminish the power of workers or be used in warfare. Some of the loudest voices in opposition are studying the arts, where human creativity is paramount, or the law, as tech companies face lawsuits over potential copyright and privacy violations.
But there are also deep concerns that A.I. degrades the experience of college itself, by removing the productive struggle of learning.

Resistors from California to Sydney to Paris are increasingly publishing manifestoes that lay out demands: that colleges not partner with A.I. companies; that professors not be required to use generative A.I. in lessons or grading; and that students be allowed to refuse to complete assignments that require the use of chatbots, without any impact on their grades.
At the University of Kentucky, a research employee who described himself as a humanist successfully applied for a religious exemption from using A.I.

Alice Beatty, 22, helped lead the Transylvania petition drive as a senior last spring. The student newspaper had called attention to the $120,000 the university paid to purchase licenses to ChatGPT and Gemini, chatbots from OpenAI and Google. And Ms. Beatty had participated in a discussion group formed by several A.I.-skeptical professors.

She noted that even before Transylvania provided free access to chatbots, A.I. had been everywhere on campus. Students used it to summarize readings, break down physics problems and compose discussion-board posts and papers that they were supposed to be writing the old-fashioned way, on their own.
Yet when Ms. Beatty and some classmates stood near the dining hall to collect signatures on the petition, almost everyone they spoke to signed.
“I use A.I.,” she recalled some peers telling her, “and I am ashamed I use it.”
A spokeswoman for Transylvania University declined an interview request but said that professors were free to either embrace A.I., limit its use or ban it entirely in their classes.
For students, ethical and practical questions about A.I. will be part of the world they enter after graduating, she said by email.

Vague and confusing college A.I. policies have helped create the conscientious objector movement, said Hollis Robbins, an English professor at the University of Utah who writes often about A.I. and education. She suggested that colleges stop grading take-home assignments that are easy to cheat on with A.I., and shut down online courses that have become rife with academic misconduct in the A.I. era.
If institutions took those steps, she argued, students might be more curious and hopeful about the technology.
“There is silence about these major tech issues,” she said. “Students just seeing grown-ups being inconsistent and letting them down.”
Georgetown University began offering students and faculty free access to Gemini in March. At the time, like many institutions, Georgetown generally allowed each professor to set their own A.I. rules.

Yet in focus groups on A.I. conducted by the university, students asked for clearer guidance. They were worried about cognitive offloading, cheating and A.I. providing false information. Forty percent of the student sentiment was cautious or negative toward A.I., according to the university, compared with 25 percent that was positive or hopeful.

Georgetown’s student newspaper published an editorial criticizing the Gemini license, arguing that it tacitly pushed students toward technology that is often used to plagiarize and avoid academic effort.

This fall, the university is changing its approach. Under a new president, Eduardo M. Peñalver, it announced it would form a faculty committee to come up with clearer principles on A.I. use. For Georgetown, a Jesuit institution, Pope Leo XIV’s recent encyclical on the risks of A.I. will be an important influence.

Dr. Peñalver said in an interview that Georgetown would seek to make course expectations around A.I. more transparent and provide more tech-free spaces on campus. Oral presentations, discussion groups and in-person tests would become more important, he said, to protect “from the intrusion of this technology.”
Still, the university will continue to expand free access to A.I. tools, which he said had the potential to do good.
“We’re not interested in pushing people to use A.I. in ways that don’t align with their values,” Dr. Peñalver said. “But I certainly encourage people to learn about it.”
“Even if you’re opposed to this technology,” he added, “that awareness and understanding is important to the success of your project.”
Many conscientious objectors, though, say they try to avoid generative A.I. as much as possible, blocking it from their devices and not experimenting with it in their own work.

Emily Tucker, executive director of the Center on Privacy and Technology at Georgetown Law School, has been a leader in organizing resistance to A.I. use on campus. She has also signed an open letter with 1,300 other educators “who refuse the call for generative A.I. adoption in schools and colleges, and reject the narrative of its inevitability.”

Law students have told her they feared that if they didn’t use A.I. to speed their output, they would be outpaced in class and at work by those who did. But Professor Tucker said that using A.I. degrades a student’s ability to read and analyze dense legal texts, and risks incorrect citations of case law.

“It’s not useful,” said Professor Tucker, who said she rarely uses A.I. herself, though she acknowledged it might help in some tasks, like seeking specific information within a large set of documents.

At Cornell, Shimon Edelman, a psychology professor who holds a Ph.D. in computer science, has also signed the anti-A.I. letter. He lets students decide whether or not to use A.I., though he warns them it could degrade deeper learning.

He said he had been dismayed to see the Cornell administration greet A.I. warmly, as an “essential tool,” instead of warning more forcefully against its risks. In October, Cornell announced free access to chatbots, A.I. coding tools and agentic A.I.
“It’s unthinkable,” Professor Edelman said of using A.I. in his own research, even when he faced having to read 800 documents for a recent book project.
Emmali Simmelink, a senior studying classics and religion at Whitman College in Washington State, said students on her campus sometimes plug classroom discussion prompts directly into ChatGPT.
“If you can’t generate a coherent thought without ChatGPT, I genuinely lose a lot of respect for you,” she said. She added, laughing, “I am really insufferable about this.”
She said she brings up concerns about the environmental impact of A.I. as soon as she hears somebody say, “I asked ChatGPT.”
The topic can be divisive socially, so much so, several students said, that friend groups often develop a shared view of A.I.

Preston Hicks, 26, is studying history and education at Rider University in New Jersey — a second degree, after he worked previously as a software developer. He said many of his friends are artists who instinctually oppose A.I., a view he often shares.
But he can also imagine using A.I. in his future career as a teacher, to handle paperwork and other logistical tasks.
“I am more nuanced,” he said. “If I see a good use, I will use it.”

news.title: US companies turn to robots to ease labour shortage crisis
news.title_en: US companies turn to robots to ease labour shortage crisis

news.summary_en: North American manufacturers are accelerating robot adoption to mitigate severe labor shortages, with Q3 2026 orders reaching 11,000 units, a 25% year-on-year increase. Notably, orders for collaborative robots (cobots) surged by 56%, serving as a critical lever for firms to scale output amid persistent workforce limitations.
paragraphs: American companies are racing to install more industrial robots in factories and warehouses, as rising costs and worsening labour shortages threaten to choke off a nascent US manufacturing boom.

North American companies ordered almost 11,000 robots in the third quarter of 2026, up 25 per cent on the same period last year, according to the Association for Advancing Automation (A3). Orders of collaborative robots, or “cobots”, rose by 56 per cent.

Peggy Johnson, chief executive of Agility, a humanoid robotics company that listed on the Nasdaq this month, said that many manufacturing firms were facing “an existential problem with the labour that they can’t get”.

“There’s an older workforce doing manual, repetitive jobs that is retiring, we have a younger workforce that is not seeking those jobs, and then we have a government that is reshoring and that’s increasing the need for those jobs,” Johnson told the FT.

Successive US administrations have used a combination of generous tax credits and punitive tariffs to encourage companies to “reshore” manufacturing amid concerns over post-industrial decline in America’s heartlands and increasing competition from China.
Along with a post-Covid desire to reduce dependence on fragile global supply chains, the push has driven hundreds of billions of dollars of investment into US manufacturing over the past decade.

But rising inflation and President Donald Trump’s erratic application of tariffs have caused spending on manufacturing-related construction to fall since 2025, while employment in the sector has remained broadly flat.

Mike Conway, a partner at McKinsey who specialises in advising industrial companies, said that rather than building new factories, most US-based manufacturers were looking to unlock the “latent capacity” in existing facilities, including through automation.
“Given the need to scale, we’re seeing automation becoming the new normal,” he said.

Industrial robots range from humanoids to robot arms, cobots and so-called “gantry robots” that can ferry goods along perpendicular axes. Advocates argue they free human employees from “dull, dirty and dangerous” tasks such as routine inspections, lifting heavy items or handling hazardous materials.

Traditionally, only very large manufacturers such as carmakers have been able to deploy robots at a scale necessary to justify their cost. But technological advances, including the ability to train robots in virtual environments, have lowered barriers to entry for much smaller companies.
Sebastian Montalvo, chief executive of Texas-based aerospace and defence supplier M3 Aerospace, said that automation would allow his company, which employs 11 staff, to grow faster with fewer people.
“How we operate now is we have one operator, one machine, but I think with technology and robotics we may have one operator, five machines,” he said.

Alex Shikany, executive vice-president of A3, noted that whereas automotive companies had historically placed the bulk of North American robot orders, non-auto sectors including logistics, agriculture, life sciences and electronics together now account for more than half the sector.
“It bodes well for the robotics industry as we move forward because it’s less reliant on just one type of customer,” he said.
However, some experts argue that the speed of automation in the US is still not fast enough to make the country internationally competitive.

Robert Atkinson, founder and senior fellow at the Information Technology and Innovation Foundation think-tank, said that with US labour costs so much higher than in China, American companies should be automating even more aggressively.

“We need to double, triple the amount of robotic automation within five to eight years, or I believe we will lose a significant share of what remains of our manufacturing to China,” he said. “But we’re nowhere near.”

Analysts note that most of the robots being installed in the US come from abroad, feeding a tension in the Trump administration’s policies between its stated desire to revive US manufacturing, and its unhappiness about a surge in robots being brought into the country.The White House said last month that the Department of Commerce had found that “robotics, industrial machinery and their components” are being imported into the US “in such quantities . . . as to threaten to impair the national security of the United States”.But it added that it was holding off on applying extra tariffs on national security grounds because the US “still produces less robotics and industrial equipment than it consumes” and “lacks the capacity to satisfy the need for robotics and industrial machinery with domestic sources”.

Experts note an irony whereby the same shortage of skills that is driving companies to automate is likely to undermine US automation efforts. According to a recent labour shortage index compiled by the Alliance For America’s Skilled Trades, technicians needed to install and maintain automated systems are in shorter supply than almost any other category of skilled worker.
Agility’s Johnson believes that demand from companies for robots that can operate at facilities designed for human workers will continue to grow.
But the ITIF’s Atkinson warns that investing in robots to eke out incremental productivity gains at old facilities will not revive American manufacturing.
“When you build new things from scratch, you put in global state of the art equipment and technology — that’s what we see the Chinese doing,” he said.
“But we’re sort of retrofitting existing plants and it’s just harder to do. Maybe in 25 or 30 years we’ll have built everything we need, but we can’t wait that long.”

news.author: Bloomberg
news.content_snippet:
Google will invest $15 billion in building infrastructure in Missouri, including a data center in New Florence, Montgomery County.

In addition to the data center, the company will work with Ameren to bring 500MW of new power capacity to the state's grid, building on the 1GW already contracted by Google in Missouri.

The two companies will also work with Evergy to bring a Capacity Commitment Framework (CCF) to Missouri, which will ensure large energy consumers, including Google, pay for their el
news.summary_en: Alphabet and Google President Ruth Porat announced a $15 billion investment in data center infrastructure in Missouri. The central project, 'Project Spade' in Montgomery County, targets a 1.2GW capacity. To address energy needs, Google is partnering with utility providers Ameren and Evergy to secure 500MW of additional grid capacity while utilizing a Capacity Commitment Framework (CCF) to protect local rate payers.
paragraphs: Google will invest $15 billion in building infrastructure in Missouri, including a data center in New Florence, Montgomery County.
In addition to the data center, the company will work with Ameren to bring 500MW of new power capacity to the state's grid, building on the 1GW already contracted by Google in Missouri.

The two companies will also work with Evergy to bring a Capacity Commitment Framework (CCF) to Missouri, which will ensure large energy consumers, including Google, pay for their electricity needs and protect local rate payers.

While the data center campus under development is known as Project Spade. Planned for a 934-acre plot of land by data center developer Related Digital, the campus is targeting 1.2GW of capacity and represents a "multi-billion-dollar" investment in the region.

The data center will use a closed-loop, air-cooled system, and limit water use to domestic needs. According to Baxtel, the data center will feature two buildings spanning around 800,000 sq ft of floor space.
Construction is expected to begin in 2026, and will see the creation of 2,000 construction jobs.

“We look forward to expanding Google’s investments in Missouri and helping Missourians benefit from the next wave of American innovation,” said Ruth Porat, president and chief investment officer of Alphabet and Google. “To deliver the upside of technology, we are investing in workforce development and energy affordability, both directly and through our partnerships with local organizations. This commitment will provide thousands of Missourians with valuable technical and trade skills, while supporting energy affordability for residents in Montgomery County and across the state."

“Google’s historic investment in Montgomery County is a testament to Missouri’s growing reputation as a premier destination for innovation and next-generation technology,” added Missouri Governor Mike Kehoe. “Beyond the significant economic impact and job creation, Google has demonstrated a true commitment to strengthening the community through local partnerships, investments, grants, and support for area businesses. This project represents more than infrastructure—it’s an investment in Missouri families, communities, and long-term opportunity. We are proud to partner with companies like Google that are helping drive economic growth while making a meaningful difference in the communities they call home.”
Elsewhere in Missouri, Google is known to be developing a data center campus in Kansas City under the "Project Kestrel" moniker, and others known as Project Shale and Project Micah.

New Florence is located east of Kansas City, between Columbia and St Louis. The area is not a typical data center location, but earlier this year, Amazon Web Services was exploring a 1,000-acre campus nearby.

news.title: Anthropic retail investors face squeeze in blockbuster IPO
news.title_en: Anthropic retail investors face squeeze in blockbuster IPO

inline_images.caption: SpaceX raised $75bn in the world’s biggest IPO © Adam Gray/Bloomberg
inline_images.alt: SpaceX raised $75bn in the world’s biggest IPO © Adam Gray/Bloomberg

news.author: Ryan McMorrow and George Steer
news.content_snippet:
Retail investors vying for a piece of Anthropic’s blockbuster listing are facing off against an avalanche of institutional demand that is likely to leave many with fewer shares than they hoped.

The AI lab has earmarked up to a fifth of its record IPO for individual investors, or nearly $19bn of stock at $83 per share. But people familiar with the matter expect the allocation to be trimmed below 20 per cent, with orders for Anthropic stock running at several times the amount of shares on offer.
news.summary_en: Anthropic aims to allocate approximately 20% of its IPO to individual investors, yet the offering has been heavily oversubscribed by institutional demand managed by JPMorgan. Despite efforts through brokers like Robinhood and Fidelity, the significant oversubscription is expected to compress the final retail allocation below the initial 20% target.
news.title_zh: Anthropic IPO零售配售份额或不足20%
news.summary_zh: 由于机构认购踊跃，Anthropic上市零售配售份额预计将低于预设的20%上限，但仍远超传统大型IPO比例
paragraphs: Retail investors vying for a piece of Anthropic’s blockbuster listing are facing off against an avalanche of institutional demand that is likely to leave many with fewer shares than they hoped.

The AI lab has earmarked up to a fifth of its record IPO for individual investors, or nearly $19bn of stock at $83 per share. But people familiar with the matter expect the allocation to be trimmed below 20 per cent, with orders for Anthropic stock running at several times the amount of shares on offer.

For the past week, online brokers in the US and abroad have been taking orders from ordinary investors and feeding that demand data back to Anthropic’s underwriters, including JPMorgan, which is running the US retail portion of the offering. Those familiar with the deal said the IPO was several times oversubscribed, signalling intense demand from institutional investors, which will probably lead the retail portion to be squeezed.

Even an allocation in the mid to high teens would far exceed the 5 to 10 per cent retail buyers have historically received in large IPOs, underscoring how individual investors have become central to bookbuilding in the era of mega listings. “We’re spending a lot of time with bankers and underwriters advocating for retail,” said Abhishek Fatehpuria, vice-president of product at Robinhood, speaking generally rather than about Anthropic. “Our mission is to get as much to retail as possible for these IPOs.”

Robinhood is one of five US brokers offering Anthropic shares to individual investors, alongside Charles Schwab, Fidelity, SoFi and E*Trade. Together the platforms hold more than $10tn in retail client assets.Day traders have grown into a powerful force in US equity markets, piling into “meme stocks”, options and leveraged exchange traded funds, a trend that has buoyed companies such as Tesla but also fuelled bouts of volatility. Anthropic’s prospectus lists the retail allocation and continuing “retail investor interest” in the stock among factors that could cause its share price to swing.
Elon Musk’s SpaceX set the template earlier this year, with the world’s richest man keen to place small shareholders near the centre of the AI and rockets group’s ownership register from the outset.

But retail investors were ultimately squeezed down to about 22 per cent of that offering, or about $19bn. Underwriters had received more than $100bn of orders on retail platforms, according to people familiar with the matter.
Robinhood says it still handed out at least one SpaceX share to all 850,000 investors who requested shares on its platform.
While Musk’s offering was pitched to his legion of devoted fans and 240mn followers on X, retail buyers of Anthropic say they are backing a product they use and believe in.
Rupok Ghosh Adin, a software engineer based in Canada, said he had subscribed for several shares through his online brokerage, his first time participating in an IPO.

Adin said he was betting on Anthropic’s AI models, which he said have won over most of the tech industry. “We all know how capable they are,” he added, noting he also had faith in chief executive Dario Amodei’s “very strong sense of purpose”.
Taylor, a 49-year-old based in St Louis, who works in web marketing, said he subscribed for 100 shares through his Robinhood brokerage account.
“We heavily use Claude at my office,” he said, asking not to include his last name. “The productivity gains are insane, but I do worry it will eventually replace us.”

So high is the demand for Anthropic shares that some in the crypto industry have blamed a slide in digital asset prices on traders selling coins to free up cash in their trading accounts. The price of bitcoin is down about 20 per cent over the past month.

Anthropic’s bankers have also taken the pitch directly to the retail audience, helping the group pull together a website for the IPO and a promotional video featuring Anthropic’s founders laying out their vision for the company.

JPMorgan chief executive Jamie Dimon hosted Amodei in a conversation streamed online and in dozens of its branches across the country last week, during which Anthropic’s chief said the advice that resonated with him was to “never let your company be worth a single dollar more than it’s really worth.”

news.summary_en: ByteDance co-founder Zhang Yiming has become the richest person in Asia with a net worth exceeding $105 billion, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index. His wealth surged following valuation markups by institutional investors like BlackRock and Fidelity, coupled with ByteDance's aggressive pivot toward AI development, including Doubao, Seedance, and a massive 10-trillion-parameter model.
paragraphs: ByteDance co-founder Zhang Yiming, in a portrait released by the company in 2021.

ByteDance co-founder Zhang Yiming is now Asia’s richest person, with an estimated fortune of more than $105bn, putting him ahead of Indian industrialist Gautam Adani, according to Bloomberg. The ranking comes from the Bloomberg Billionaires Index, and Zhang, 43, has never held the top spot before.

The figure is an estimate, and other trackers disagree. Forbes’ real-time list put Zhang’s net worth at $84bn on Wednesday. The gap comes largely from how each list values ByteDance, a private company whose shares do not trade publicly. Bloomberg applies a 10% risk discount to its valuation.

Investor valuations drove the latest jump. Zhang’s wealth rose by more than $12bn this month after Bloomberg analyzed the latest marks that BlackRock, Fidelity Investments, and T. Rowe Price put on their ByteDance holdings. In June, the index had already lifted him past Mukesh Ambani into second place, after Bloomberg cut its ByteDance discount from 25% once the company’s US restructuring was settled.

That restructuring nearly went the other way. ByteDance spent much of last year facing a possible US shutdown of TikTok, before handing control of the app’s American business to a venture led by Oracle and Silver Lake in January. Since then, the company has leaned harder into AI, with the Doubao chatbot and the Seedance video generator, alongside a 10-trillion-parameter model now in training.
“He plays his cards right,” Lian Jye Su, chief analyst at research firm Omdia, told Bloomberg.“He stayed on course and then continued to double down on AI investment.”

Su said Zhang kept backing AI development even as US lawmakers questioned TikTok chief executive Shou Chew in 2023, and that ByteDance’s store of social media data could in theory help it train models.
He called AI ByteDance’s biggest opportunity since its video platform, and fierce competition in China its biggest risk.

Adani’s slide explains the other half of the swap. His fortune peaked at about $120bn in June, Bloomberg reported, before an MSCI index rebalancing wiped about $15bn off his group’s market value at the end of August. A wider selloff, driven by rising oil prices and bond yields, pushed the shares lower still.

Zhang’s estimated wealth has grown about eightfold since March 2019, when Bloomberg first valued it at $13bn. He was already China’s richest person, and he now sits above Adani, Ambani, and Uniqlo founder Tadashi Yanai, fortunes built on ports, energy, and retail. The same boom has also made founders of Chinese chipmakers billionaires, even though those companies have yet to turn a profit, Bloomberg reported last week.

The ranking lands in a week when Beijing has been publicly defending its AI ambitions. China’s commerce ministry dismissed calls by US AI executives to slow frontier development as a bid for technological hegemony, and China’s richest person, whose fortune increasingly rests on AI, is now also Asia’s richest person.

news.summary_en: Financial experts, including former SEC Chair Gary Gensler, are warning of a significant speculative bubble in AI stocks. The core concern centers on the widening gap between massive capital expenditures in AI infrastructure and actual generated returns, exacerbated by circular financing and high debt, raising the specter of a market crash.
paragraphs: The artificial intelligence (AI) boom began in earnest when OpenAI introduced ChatGPT in November 2022. Since then, the S&P 500 (^GSPC -0.23%) and Nasdaq Composite (^IXIC +0.42%) have advanced 90% and 122%, respectively, as investors have poured money into companies developing AI chips, infrastructure, and software.

However, the enthusiasm has been accompanied by a growing chorus of warnings that AI stocks are in a speculative bubble. And several prominent financial experts think the boom will end with a devastating stock market crash, potentially dragging the U.S. economy into a recession.
Those concerns deserve consideration, and some arguments have merit, but Wall Street's doomsayers seem to be ignoring crucial facts about the stock market's valuation and the economic benefits of AI.
Image source: OpenAI (AI-generated illustration).

Former SEC Chair Gary Gensler recently warned that artificial intelligence had already formed a stock market bubble that could burst and trigger a recession before the 2028 presidential election. In an interview with CNN, he expressed concern about the massive amount of money being invested in AI infrastructure, particularly the growing reliance on debt and complex financing deals.

Admittedly, Gensler makes good points, and he is not alone. Michael Burry, the investor who famously predicted the collapse of the U.S. housing market in 2008, has also warned that technology companies are spending too much relative to profits they are likely to earn. "It is just an asset bubble, plain and simple," he wrote earlier this year. "This, all of it, is the scene of the bloody car crash, minutes before it happens."

Meanwhile, Jeremy Grantham, co-founder of investment management firm GMO, had this to say in a research paper published earlier this year: "The rule from history is that great technological innovations lead to great bubbles." And investment manager John Hussman believes the S&P 500 could eventually fall between 50% and 75% when the bubble bursts.

These warnings share several common themes. Technology companies are spending an unprecedented amount of money on AI infrastructure, often without a clear timeline for generating returns. Circular financing deals create additional risk, and investors may be overestimating the long-term profitability of AI.
Additionally, many analysts believe stocks are too expensive, and they are quick to point out a particular valuation metric has reached levels last seen during the dot-com bubble.

One metric frequently cited by market bears is the S&P 500's cyclically adjusted price-to-earnings (CAPE) ratio, which divides stock prices by average inflation-adjusted earnings over the past decade. The S&P 500's CAPE ratio topped 40 in six consecutive months this year, a level last seen when the dot-com bubble burst in 2000.

However, CAPE is a backward-looking valuation metric. That means it does not account for future earnings growth, which is particularly important when evaluating a transformative technology like AI. Indeed, forward-looking valuation metrics tell a very different story.

The S&P 500's forward price-to-earnings (PE) ratio rocketed by 20 and eventually topped 25 as the dot-com bubble built momentum in the late 1990s. That happened because stock prices were appreciating much faster than corporate profits were increasing. The S&P 500's forward PE ratio stayed above 22 until early 2001.

The opposite is happening today. The S&P 500's forward PE ratio topped 23 last year, but the valuation has gradually moderated as earnings growth has accelerated. Today, the S&P 500 trades at 17.7 times forward earnings, according to FactSet Research. That is the cheapest valuation in more than three years, and it's a discount to the 10-year average of 18.9.

That doesn't sound like a bubble. Of course, that argument depends on companies meeting Wall Street's earnings estimates. But investors have several reasons to believe corporate profits can continue to grow rapidly.

First, AI adoption is happening at an extraordinary pace. The Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis found that generative AI reached 55% of U.S. adults ages 18 to 64 approximately three years after ChatGPT launched. At comparable stages, personal computers and the internet had adoption rates of just 20% and 30%, respectively.
Second, AI is already generating measurable economic benefits, despite being relatively early in its adoption cycle.

There are many other examples. Businesses are already using the technology to reduce costs, boost productivity, and create true value. As adoption broadens and applications improve, those benefits could translate into sustained corporate earnings growth.

Of course, none of this means every AI stock is cheap, nor does it guarantee that the stock market will continue rising. Whether a stock is reasonably valued today ultimately depends on how quickly earnings grow tomorrow. But I do not believe there is decisive evidence that AI stocks are in an epic bubble destined to burst with catastrophic consequences. That is certainly possible, but it is not a foregone conclusion.

news.title: I Spent a Year Talking to Anthropic Employees. Here’s What They Believe.
news.title_en: I Spent a Year Talking to Anthropic Employees. Here’s What They Believe.
news.author: Jasmine Sun
news.content_snippet:

news.summary_en: As Anthropic prepares for a landmark IPO, internal concerns regarding the risks of 'recursive self-improvement' have intensified, with staff forecasting the arrival of superhuman AI researchers as early as 2027. paragraphs: Imagine an artificial intelligence company that is about to launch the biggest I.P.O. in history. Behind it are the sleepless weeks, the training runs full of bugs, the yearslong grind of wooing investors and customers without a product or profit. It will no longer be a scrappy start-up but the consummate envy of Silicon Valley. You might expect relief and celebration, champagne-drenched galas and shiny sports cars rolling into the office parking lot.

On Anthropic’s investor roadshow, there are hints of such jubilance. The Wall Street bankers ushering Anthropic into the public markets hyped a conversation with the chief executive, Dario Amodei, with music by the electronic producer Fred Again and a room adorned with futuristic Anthropic swag. But euphoria is not the mood back at Anthropic headquarters.

In the weeks leading up to the initial public offering, employees of Anthropic — who affectionately call themselves “Ants” — have been preoccupied with concerns about how to slow down A.I. Following a recent spate of rogue agent episodes, the industry has felt doomier than ever.

Even the most ardent techno-optimists have quieted their cheers. Group chats and gatherings instead debate pacing the frontier: how the leading A.I. labs can stop racing and agree to cooperate on the speed of model development, ensuring they have time to make the models safe before releasing them to the world.

For many Ants, the hard part is just beginning. They see recursive self-improvement, in which current A.I. models autonomously build the next generation, looming on the horizon. Because of this potential breakthrough, Anthropic’s co-founder Jack Clark as well as the independent forecasting group A.I. Futures Project have moved up the likely arrival date for superhuman A.I. researchers. They now anticipate it being in 2027.

Once A.I. models can build their successors, they are even more likely to escape human control. Nobody is ready for this future, but nobody is stopping — rather the opposite. Anthropic’s first spending priority with its I.P.O. cash will be buying more compute to reach recursive self-improvement before its rivals do.

I have spoken to dozens of Ants during the past two years, from company founders to young researchers to jaded ex-employees. I have found them surprisingly earnest in their dedication to making A.I. go well. But their concerns are also idiosyncratic and insular, often far removed from the concerns that most people hold about A.I.
They do not view Anthropic as a normal for-profit company. So as the U.S. economy and our personal financial fates become yoked to the Ants, it’s critical that we understand what they believe.

Juxtaposed with what they presume will be the imminent arrival of superintelligence, the upcoming payday seems parochial to many at Anthropic. Some employees describe the I.P.O. with a shrug, likening it to just another funding round.

This is a peculiar attitude for a crowd of young people who, in many cases, are about to become deca- and centimillionaires overnight. The Ants are not your average tech workers. They spend morning to night at rows of desks in the bare, high-security offices in San Francisco’s downtown, where the common books on display include Richard Rhodes’s “The Making of the Atomic Bomb” and paperback printouts of company writings, such as Mr. Amodei’s “Machines of Loving Grace” and the in-house philosopher Amanda Askell’s “Claude’s Constitution.”

No one is compelled to work the grueling “996” hours (9 a.m. to 9 p.m., six days a week) that have become common in the tech industry, but a good number of Ants do so anyway out of their own feverish devotion. Many cram themselves into modest group apartments, host house parties where few, if any, drink and blank when I ask how they spend their lavish salaries, even with my prompts: “A wardrobe update, maybe?” “Ever considered flying business class?”
The money is secondary. The most common form of I.P.O. talk involves discussions of where to allocate the newly liquid stock in their charitable donation accounts.

As a company, Anthropic has been strongly influenced by effective altruism, which holds the belief that the wealthy are obliged to share their fruits with the world. New hires are invited to pledge a percentage of their equity to charity when they start, which Anthropic matches part of. Top targets include charities dedicated to animal welfare, global health and research on A.I. alignment and safety. Many have begun giving big to political campaigns.

As for their own stock, few of the Ants I spoke to planned to sell right after the I.P.O. The notion of an “A.I. bubble” seems not to exist at Anthropic. Employees expect their equity to eventually be worth much, much more.

Anthropic crisply embodies the mind-rending paradox of contemporary A.I. The research scientists who’ve done the most to extend A.I. capabilities are often the most insistent about its risks. Anthropic is the most vocal company when it comes to economic impacts such as mass automation, yet it’s also the leading vendor of the A.I. enterprise agents that threaten to replace white-collar workers.

Such a stance can seem duplicitous and self-serving, both convenient and convoluted. “Our ability to have a positive impact on the world scales in relation to our reach and stature as a successful company,” reads one eye-roll-inducing statement in Anthropic’s I.P.O. prospectus. While the company’s leaders have been candid about the risks, they have been less forthcoming about their solutions. When asked why they should birth what they suspect is an existentially dangerous technology, their answer amounts to, essentially, just trust us because we’re the good guys.

Anthropic is about to become one of the most important companies of the 21st century. If it wants to steward our country, our economy and our lives, Anthropic must do much more to earn the public’s trust. We need a plan for how it will build A.I. safely, and not just reliance on a few people’s judgment calls.

Mr. Amodei seems to hold two convictions very strongly: First, that powerful A.I. might destroy humanity. Second, that our only shot at survival is to create a supremely successful, market-eating technology company to build that A.I. first.

Anthropic used to insist that it was not gunning for first place. In a 2022 podcast, Mr. Amodei said Anthropic “shouldn’t be racing ahead or trying to build models that are way bigger than other orgs.” He suggested instead that the company would do safety research as a fast-follower of A.I. development. The company intended to study the technology without pushing capabilities ahead, some investors said he told them at the time.

In the summer of 2022, Anthropic decided not to make Claude, its A.I. chatbot, available to the public over internal concerns about safety. This allowed OpenAI — which had gotten wind of Anthropic’s internal prototype — to design a similar product, rush ChatGPT out the door first and gain a decisive lead in consumer mindshare.

In Anthropic company lore, this saga is put on a pedestal as an example of choosing principle over profit. Yet it may have also been a strategic wake-up call for Mr. Amodei, who called the sacrifice a “one-off.” Increasingly, Mr. Amodei seemed to see how being the leader in the A.I. race conferred compounding benefits in terms of revenue, recruiting, fund-raising and developing the next-generation A.I. models. Once commercial A.I. products had been introduced, Mr. Amodei seemed unwilling to settle for second place.
Anthropic is certainly very good at racing. Although it spent its toddler years scrambling to replicate OpenAI’s language and reasoning models, Anthropic has since led the charge on coding agents.

It is not an exaggeration to say that Claude Code reinvented the discipline of software engineering. Where programmers used to write lines of code by hand, many now use plain English to command fleets of A.I. agents. Since the release of Claude Code, Anthropic’s quarterly revenue has surpassed OpenAI’s, surging to $17 billion in the third quarter of 2026. Today, more than half of the Fortune 500 are Anthropic’s six-figure customers.

With this kind of success, Mr. Amodei has updated his theory of change — he calls it a “race to the top.” Only by building the most advanced A.I. systems can Anthropic influence the whole industry in a safer direction, he argues. Three underlying assumptions are baked into this strategy.

First, Anthropic assumes the A.I. race itself is inevitable, so no single actor can stop superintelligence from being built. The financial rewards for building a machine that can match or exceed humans’ cognitive abilities are so great that someone is guaranteed to pursue it. If not Mr. Amodei and his team, then Sam Altman, or Mark Zuckerberg or Elon Musk.

Second, Anthropic assumes it is the most responsible of A.I.’s possible stewards. In public and internally, Mr. Amodei likes to invoke OpenAI and the Chinese government as competitive boogeymen. These are viewed as actors that are pushing just as hard as Anthropic on building and commercializing powerful A.I. models, but that would be far less responsible — reckless at best, and authoritarian at worst. Looking at the recent evidence, the most severe rogue agent hacks have indeed come out of OpenAI. And if you think Claude is the A.I. with the best moral values, then expanding Claude’s market share could be construed as a virtue in itself.

Third, Anthropic assumes the “winner” of A.I. will gain tremendous influence over the A.I. ecosystem and the U.S. government. Through commercial success, Anthropic aims to show the industry that being safety-minded can be good for business, good for science and good for attracting top talent.

Some Anthropic staffers point to initiatives like embedding A.I. safety auditors with the company’s engineering teams — a decision that has inspired competitors to make similar commitments. Additionally, the company has said it will use its commercial strength to advocate A.I. regulation, as it did in the fight for California’s S.B. 53, which increased transparency requirements for leading A.I. companies.

Anthropic’s race-to-the-top argument sounds positive-sum, but its worldview also contains a dose of realpolitik. In the future, it may use access to frontier A.I. systems as hard leverage in deals. “Dario talks about how Anthropic might become more powerful than the government, and needs to have its own relationship with nation-states,” said one former employee, who remained anonymous in order to discuss internal deliberations.

One former Ant referenced J.R.R. Tolkien’s parable in trying to explain Anthropic’s mind-set: Whomever builds superintelligence first will get Sauron’s ring. That person or company will possess the most dangerous cyberweapons in the world, the cures and recipes for every disease, and an army of tireless digital geniuses to do its bidding. The most load-bearing question, then, is the morality of the one who wields the ring. (Of course, in Middle Earth, the Ring was destroyed because even the purest soul couldn’t make it safe.)

And why is Anthropic confident that its own power won’t corrupt? The company prides itself on costly signals: making choices that trade off against short-term profits, whether prohibiting Chinese entities from buying its products; placing 5 percent of its shares into a “Public Benefit Fund” to spend on “large donations to traditional nonprofits or direct distributions to specific populations” of its choice; or refusing to permit the Department of Defense to use Claude for domestic mass surveillance, an act that infuriated the Trump administration and briefly got Anthropic marked as a supply-chain risk last winter.

Another former Anthropic employee explained how Mr. Amodei often justified controversial decisions, such as taking investments from Persian Gulf countries. This money, like most of the investment flowing into Anthropic, would be used to fund its sprint. The former Ant recalled Mr. Amodei saying that his goal was not to be popular with average Americans, but to do the right thing.

Anthropic has warned investors that these decisions may get more costly over time. As it details in its I.P.O. prospectus: “Our product and investment decisions may not prioritize short-term financial results,” and this “could adversely affect the market price” of the company’s stock.

The company wants to preserve the option to pivot from maximizing shareholder value to A.I. slowdowns once it assesses that the risks are too great — a strategy sometimes called “burning a lead.” Most former employees whom I spoke to believed that Mr. Amodei was deeply principled and would be willing to make sacrifices for safety. But they also acknowledged that rapid growth, and the economic momentum that propels it, can outrun even the most conscientious of founders.

Anthropic is known for its committed esprit de corps, which the S-1 Securities and Exchange Commission registration form lists as a core competitive advantage. Good Ants are dutiful, self-scrutinizing and total believers in A.I.’s world-historic importance. One notorious interview question asks employment candidates how they’d feel about working at Anthropic if their stock went to zero as a result of safety slowdowns. Research teams will happily reject technical superstars if they lack culture fit.

In internal debates, early employees act as informal ethos-enforcers, questioning whether their colleagues’ decisions are sufficiently “aligned.” It’s a company of loyalists: Both leaks and departures have been rare. Arguably, this focus has paid off. Anthropic has progressed quickly on automated coding while OpenAI, whose culture is understood to resemble a bunch of battling fiefs, was distracted by drama and side quests.

Even before the I.P.O., Anthropic has been showing signs of widening organizational fracture: It’s starting to behave like a normal company, and not everyone likes it. Some Ants fumed at the company’s Washington lobbyists for shopping a draft bill that would pre-empt state legislation on A.I. and limit the government’s ability to block model releases. Mr. Amodei mounted a public defense with a long post on X, and, in another X post, the policy team promised revisions.

Early employees mutter about cultural dilution. They question whether some of the more recently hired Ants, many of whom do regular corporate jobs, such as sales and marketing, are adequately “A.G.I.-pilled.” Do they really believe in superintelligence, or are they just trying to get rich?

Some anxious Ants have begun asking whether Anthropic should stop training better frontier models now, even if it can’t guarantee that competitors like OpenAI will do the same. This suggestion was shut down by Mr. Amodei, who urged staff members to stop listening to outside activists and explained that the company could pace itself without shooting itself in the foot. It was all part of the same strategy: Anthropic must keep winning to keep the world safe, and even if it stops, its competitors will not.

Still, grumbles from the staff reflect a growing tension between safety and growth — one that could be exacerbated by the fiduciary responsibilities of being a public company. Once Anthropic’s shares arrive in Americans’ retirement portfolios, will this new constituency really let it slow down? Will the company permit itself? Will the government? And does the company’s impact on people’s pocketbooks factor into its public-minded mission?

Anthropic hopes its public benefit corporation status will protect it against normal company incentives. Under its five-tier stock structure, the founders, employees and trustees can elect board members, while traditional investors have a limited role. The company is also trying to secure a congressional antitrust exemption so that it can coordinate a slowdown with the other American A.I. labs.

I do not doubt these good intentions. But time after time, the idealistic hopes of A.I. leaders — for instance, Anthropic’s early aim to do safety from second place, or OpenAI’s original nonprofit board — have looked naïve once faced with market realities.

There is one more big open question in the A.I. safety community: Is it technically possible to verify whether an A.I. model is aligned enough to release? This is the crux of the disagreement between Anthropic and many of its A.I. safety critics. Anthropic thinks it will be able to ship safe-enough models with careful evaluation and procedural safeguards. Skeptics see this endeavor as futile, pointing to examples of Claude only pretending to follow its instructions, or agents that have knowingly cheated and hacked during internal tests.

There is a parallel to be drawn here: We don’t have the science to determine whether an A.I. model is obedient or merely feigning compliance. At the same time, we don’t know whether a C.E.O. is altruistic and mission-driven or performative and power-hungry. But we can observe, from the history of rogue A.I.s and rogue executives, that competitive situations drive unethical behavior.

We also know that both A.I.s and founders are rewarded for extreme levels of persistence and hubris. Once committed to a mission — even a supremely risky one like building an aligned superintelligence — they will do anything but concede.

paragraphs: Lenovo Group Ltd. reported a stronger-than-expected 48% surge in second-quarter revenue, propelled by soaring enterprise demand for artificial intelligence servers and cloud computing infrastructure.

Revenue for the three months ended September 30 climbed to $30.24 billion, handily beating the $27.6 billion average estimate compiled by analysts. The top-line performance keeps the Beijing-based tech giant firmly on track to achieve its $100 billion annual revenue target.

The exceptional revenue beat was driven by Lenovo's Infrastructure Solutions Group (ISG), which encompasses data center systems and AI server deployments. ISG revenue surged 178% year-on-year to reach a record $11.3 billion, bolstered by a more than 300% jump in GPU server sales to global cloud hyperscalers.

Total AI-related sales across the enterprise—spanning specialized computing hardware, high-performance storage, and hybrid AI workstations—expanded by 79% year-on-year to $10.8 billion, representing 36% of the company's total group turnover.

While adjusted operating net income jumped 166% to $1.36 billion reflecting robust commercial momentum, the company recorded a statutory accounting loss under HKFRS due to non-cash fair-value revaluations of derivative liabilities linked to warrants and strategic partnership bonds.

Chairman and Chief Executive Officer Yang Yuanqing stated that enterprise AI transformation is transitioning from experimental pilot phases to full-scale infrastructure deployments, creating sustained tailwinds for Lenovo's hybrid AI ecosystem across server clusters and smart client devices.

news.author: Reuters
news.content_snippet:
NEW YORK, Nov 18 (Reuters) - Meta’s AI agent Muse, embodied by a smiley, fuzzy mascot named Jolly, has burrowed into encrypted personal messages, supplied made-up information about purchases and sent users chats seemingly meant for other people, a fraught start for a bot meant to simplify life for consumers, according to internal company posts reviewed by Reuters.

The unbidden actions by Muse – one of the fastest-growing apps on record, with more than 10 million downloads since its September la
news.summary_en: Meta's AI agent Muse has exhibited critical functional errors, including unauthorized access to third-party push notifications, disclosure of private bank balances, and cross-account data leakage. Internal reports indicate that Muse defaults to reading Android push notifications, enabling it to ingest data from encrypted services like Signal without explicit user authorization.
paragraphs: NEW YORK, Nov 18 (Reuters) - Meta’s AI agent Muse, embodied by a smiley, fuzzy mascot named Jolly, has burrowed into encrypted personal messages, supplied made-up information about purchases and sent users chats seemingly meant for other people, a fraught start for a bot meant to simplify life for consumers, according to internal company posts reviewed by Reuters.

The unbidden actions by Muse – one of the fastest-growing apps on record, with more than 10 million downloads since its September launch, and the centerpiece of Meta’s plan to generate billions of dollars in AI revenue – have prompted unnerved employees to raise concerns it could be mixing up conversations between different accounts and exposing users’ private data, the posts showed.

In some of those cases, Meta staffers reported the agent sending them messages about a childcare request they had not made, career advice they had not sought, product orders they had not placed and bank account balances that were not theirs.

In one post, from earlier this month, an employee told colleagues his Muse had randomly added an extra message to its regular chats about fishing-related weather and tide information, saying: “BTW, two bank updates, your Capital One balance is $2722.58, your Charles Schwab balance is $5899.57.”
“I have never shared my bank account with Muse and never discussed any banking topic with Muse. I’m afraid it’s sending other’s bank info to me,” the staffer wrote in his post.

In another example, an employee using Muse on her personal phone reported it had surprised her with a reminder to respond to a message from her sister on Signal, an end-to-end encrypted messaging service popular with privacy advocates that competes with Meta’s WhatsApp.
“This seems like an extreme privacy violation. I definitely did not grant it access to other apps, or recall being asked about this,” the employee said in her post.

A colleague responded, saying he had discovered Muse was set up by default with permission to access push notifications on phones with Google’s Android operating system after being similarly caught off guard by unsolicited chats related to apps he had not connected.

For this story, Reuters reviewed more than two dozen internal posts describing undesired actions by Muse since its debut, many of them from a feedback group where Meta employees flag problems to the team building the agent. Reuters also worked with staff at Signal and the AI Now Institute, a non-profit that studies AI’s impact on society, to replicate Muse’s access to Signal messages. The results of those tests indicated the issue described by the Meta employees was ongoing and could be affecting others.

In response to questions about Signal access and other Muse safety concerns, Meta spokesperson Daniel Roberts described the Reuters examples as “isolated incidents,” saying the company prioritizes safety, conducts extensive internal testing and continuously updates products to improve protections.

Muse needs to see and interact with people’s computers in order to work on their behalf, and can access other apps only via permissions they explicitly grant, Roberts said. He said many of the messages flagged by employees as potential account mix-ups were hallucinations, a term referring to AI models’ tendency to make things up, and had already been addressed.
Reuters was unable to establish whether Muse was giving users other people’s bank account balances and other sensitive data, or making up the information.

The Muse incidents highlight the risks associated with an emerging category of consumer AI agents hitting the market from Meta, OpenAI and others, pitched as the next big wave of AI technology. The bots promise to reshape how digital exchanges operate by executing time-saving tasks like answering emails, booking appointments and making online purchases without direct instructions.

Meta is ahead of competitors so far, with Muse consistently topping app download charts after heavy promotion to the company’s more than 3.6 billion users on Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp. The app’s retention rate is also strong, with around a quarter of the people who have set up Muse accounts returning to use it each day, the company has disclosed.

To work effectively, agents need deep access to smartphones and computers. However, they are also prone to making mistakes, exploiting obscure loopholes and accomplishing their objectives in sometimes harmful ways. OpenAI and Anthropic, for instance, have revealed instances of their AI agents unexpectedly hacking other companies and weakening systems designed to monitor their activities.

Some banks and retailers have responded to those risks by blocking agents. The technology is also posing new challenges for operating system providers like Apple and Google, which manage the permissions agents use to navigate around people’s devices. Apple, for instance, changed its operating system this week to give people more control over agents’ data usage after an Inc. Magazine columnist accused Muse of reading private chats from the Messages app on his Mac.

Meta has assured Muse users it isolates each agent in its own secure “virtual machine” – a cloud-based emulation of a personal computer – and gives people full control over which apps they connect. Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg has cited those protections in dismissing calls for industry-wide AI safety standards, arguing companies already have incentives to build safe products, both to earn consumers’ trust and avoid legal risks. Even so, Meta warns incoming users Muse may make mistakes and its terms of service hold users responsible for the agent’s actions.

To find out how Muse might access encrypted messages without users’ knowledge, Reuters provided a description of the Meta employee’s post – where the bot randomly prompted her to respond to a Signal message – to staff at Signal and the AI Now Institute. Reuters then worked with them to replicate the access she had observed.

Testers prompted Muse to read Signal messages on different operating systems. On an Android phone and an Apple laptop, it responded by bypassing Meta’s “Connector” tool and instead using permissions granted during the bot’s initial setup to pull in the message text, leveraging those authorizations in ways a user might not anticipate.

Specifically, on Android, it used its permission to access the device's push notifications to retrieve the messages, just as the Meta employees had described. On Apple’s macOS, it used a combination of the computer’s accessibility and screenshot tools, repurposing settings Apple offers to help people with disabilities operate their computers.
The same requests were blocked in tests conducted on an iPhone.
The results indicate Meta is interpreting the permissions granted by Muse users broadly, an approach that has long earned the company criticism from privacy advocates and hefty fines from regulators.

In response to Reuters’ findings, Signal President Meredith Whittaker accused Meta of launching Muse “without showing any respect for basic privacy or cybersecurity,” calling the deployment of agents that can gain wide access to people’s devices “technologically reckless.”

She called for app developers like Signal to be given “consistent technical ways” to mark their applications as off-limits to AI agents, for Meta and other AI companies to honor those boundaries and for operating system providers to enforce the rules.

Presented with the same findings, Apple and Google said they were considering changes to give people more control over what they authorize with AI agents – though Google, like Meta, noted that people already “must deliberately grant permissions” for apps to access Android notifications.

Apple said it had built its accessibility tools for people with disabilities and cautioned that leveraging them “for unintended purposes” could put people’s personal information at risk. Its operating system update this week effectively closed the pathway identified by Reuters, sharply restricting developers’ use of accessibility tools on Macs and introducing a new agent-oriented set of permissions.
“We are committed to ensuring users understand exactly what they are allowing, so they can make informed choices about their data and privacy,” Apple said in a statement.

In other cases discussed internally, staffers reported cases of Muse informing users about transactions that never occurred and making up prices on products they did purchase, costing them real money. In one incident, the agent booked a non-refundable Airbnb stay without permission, an employee reported.

Some of the incidents that raised the most concern involved cryptic out-of-context messages sent by the agent that appeared to contain other people’s information, in many cases phrased as replies to queries the users had never submitted.

In a late September social media post, a member of Meta’s Superintelligence team behind Muse initially described a user report of a similar problem as a temporary hallucination-related glitch, resolved the same day it arose. However, the internal posts reviewed by Reuters showed such incidents occurring as far back as mid-September and continuing through this month.
In one such post, an employee reported his Muse sending him a message “out of nowhere” saying it was unable to submit a request related to a parent’s control over who could access their child’s data.
He had done nothing to trigger the chat, and had never discussed child data or caregiving access with his Muse, he said.
When he asked Muse about the message, the bot replied: “I don’t have a good explanation for it other than that it wasn’t related to our conversation. Let’s ignore it. How can I help?”

Another staffer said Muse randomly offered to “message the seller” about picking up a coffee table. When the employee asked Muse, “What are you talking about?” the agent responded that it had “pulled in some context about a coffee table pickup that doesn’t seem to be yours.”
This was “not my conversation,” the employee said in his post, expressing concern about a “possible cross-account context leak.”

To address employee worries, another Superintelligence team member told the internal feedback group in early November that the agent appeared to be hallucinating messages in response to built-in prompts pushing it to engage with users in between sessions.

“These (hallucinations) unfortunately bias towards the most uncomfortable topics, like finances/security/safety, which sucks,” he said, adding that he was aware of several other cases involving “crypto-related things too, like giving people updates on their Bitcoin balances.”
He said the issues involved both the underlying AI model and the software enabling Muse to take actions, and that the team was working through them.
Roberts declined to answer Reuters questions about those issues, including how many there were and why they were persisting.

SUZHOU, China, Nov. 19, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- MegaRobo Technologies (MegaRobo), a technology company building Intelligence Infrastructure for the Physical World, today announced that it has raised nearly US$200 million in a new financing round joined by Oman Investment Authority (OIA), the sovereign wealth fund of the Sultanate of Oman.
